essential points about responsibility, perception, and the totality of circumstances, especially when an armed civilian inserts himself into an active law‑enforcement operation. Even if a person has the legal right to carry, that right carries an ethical obligation to avoid escalating tensions, to comply immediately with commands, and to stay clear of police actions. Approaching officers during an enforcement operation—while armed—and engaging in verbal confrontation creates confusion and risk, and officers must interpret that behavior through the lens of potential threat. Once resistance begins, especially physical resistance, officers have to consider whether the individual is trying to access his own weapon, attempting to grab an officer’s weapon, or escalating toward deadly force. The unanswered questions—whether he reached for the gun, whether he verbally threatened them, whether he attempted to interfere with their weapons—are exactly what shape the “reasonable officer” standard. Under that standard, the legality and justification of force depend on what a reasonable officer would perceive in that moment, not on hindsight. If he was reaching for a firearm or making lethal threats, the response would be evaluated one way; if he was not, it would be evaluated another. That is why the answer is not absolute but depends on the full context, the behavior observed, and the rapidly evolving circumstances that officers had to interpret in real time.
